first_impression.reaction: My daughter sent this with 'Mum, is this the form we need?' The first paragraph tells me what it is, when it's due and that without it there's no wedding. Plain English, no gushing. Then it says if they marry overseas instead, this form doesn't apply. That's the bit I actually need to understand before we spend anything, so I'll keep going.

journey.quote: Without it, the marriage cannot go ahead.
journey.reaction: Right. That's the sentence that tells me this matters and isn't something to leave to the last minute.

journey.quote: If you plan to marry legally in another country instead, the NOIM does not come into it: you follow that country's rules.
journey.reaction: Good to have that up front. I'd assumed every Australian couple filled this in regardless. Now I know there's a choice to make first.

journey.quote: Destination couples either marry legally in Australia and celebrate abroad, which needs a NOIM, or marry legally abroad under local rules, often with a Certificate of No Impediment.
journey.reaction: Long sentence for a summary, and 'Certificate of No Impediment' is new to me. I got the gist but only properly understood it further down.

journey.section: When do you need to lodge your NOIM?
journey.quote: Treat that as a floor, not a target.
journey.reaction: Sensible advice. I'll be repeating that to my daughter, who leaves everything to the week before.

journey.section: Who can witness a Notice of Intended Marriage?
journey.quote: If you are outside Australia, your authorised witness must also be outside Australia, and cannot be a celebrant.
journey.reaction: Useful if her partner is still working in London. Clear rule, clearly stated.

journey.quote: Keep the originals together in one folder. The same birth certificate and passport often come back into play later, when you apply for your official marriage certificate or change your name.
journey.reaction: That's the kind of practical tip I like. It sounds like someone who's actually done this.

journey.section: Can the one-month notice be shortened?
journey.quote: A prescribed authority is an officer or employee of the Commonwealth, a state or a territory, appointed by the Attorney-General.
journey.reaction: This section gets a bit government-handbook. I skimmed it. Still, 'Approval is never automatic' is the honest bit and I appreciated that.

journey.section: NOIM or marrying abroad: which paperwork applies?
journey.quote: You hold a small legal ceremony in Australia with an authorised celebrant, and the NOIM applies exactly as above.
journey.reaction: Now this is what I'd want. Do the legal part here, properly, with family who can't fly, then the big celebration overseas. My mother could come to the small one without a long-haul flight.

journey.quote: DFAT can issue a CNI in Australia, but some local authorities accept only CNIs issued in their own country. Ask the destination's embassy or consulate whether you need a CNI, where to get it, and whether it needs an authentication or apostille.
journey.reaction: This is where my heart sinks a little. Embassies, apostilles, certificates that may or may not be accepted. It's thorough, but it makes Option A sound much less risky, and I wonder who holds the kids' hands through this if they choose Option B.

journey.quote: Either way, the legal steps stay with you and your celebrant or the local authority. The celebration is where we come in.
journey.reaction: At least that's straight. I know who's responsible for what. I'd rather be told that than have someone pretend they do everything.

journey.quote: Your Wedded Advisor is a single point of contact who plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments for the celebration abroad, works in your time zone and quotes in AUD, with the fee agreed in writing before any work begins
journey.reaction: One person, our time zone, Australian dollars, the fee in writing first. That's what I'd forward to my husband.

unanswered_questions: If they choose to marry legally abroad, does the Wedded Advisor at least keep track of the paperwork timeline alongside the venue, or is that entirely on my daughter?
If they do the small legal ceremony here first, can the Wedded Advisor plan around that date so the overseas celebration lines up?
Is the first step a phone call with a real person before anything is booked or paid?

turn_offs_found.quote: Many countries ask you to prove you are not already married. The most common documents are a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage (CNI) and certificates from a registry of births, deaths and marriages, and some countries add rules such as a residence period. Local authorities may also ask for divorce papers, a deceased spouse's death certificate, and your original birth certificate and passport.
turn_offs_found.why: It runs straight on into another long paragraph of DFAT, embassies and apostilles, then a third full of links. On the iPad it's a wall of text, and it's the most important part for us. A few short points would help me print it for my husband.

turn_offs_found.quote: Destination couples either marry legally in Australia and celebrate abroad, which needs a NOIM, or marry legally abroad under local rules, often with a Certificate of No Impediment.
turn_offs_found.why: A takeaway should be the easy bit. This one packs two routes and an unexplained certificate into one line, so I had to read it twice.

would_share_with: My daughter, with 'Treat that as a floor, not a target' and the keep-the-originals-in-one-folder tip
My husband, with Option A (legal ceremony here, celebration abroad) and the Wedded Advisor paragraph (AUD, fee in writing)

cta_reaction.quote: One Wedded Advisor plans the venue, travel, vendors and payments with you as a single point of contact, anywhere in the world, and confirms the inclusions in writing before you commit.
cta_reaction.why: It says the right things: one person, inclusions in writing before we commit. But this article is about a form, and my daughter hasn't decided which route yet. I'd click once they've settled that, and I'd want a phone call with a real person first.

top_3_changes: Break the Option B paragraphs ('Many countries ask you to prove...' and 'DFAT can issue a CNI...') into short points: what you may need, who to ask, what to check. It's the most decision-critical part and currently the densest.

Split the key takeaway 'Destination couples either marry legally in Australia and celebrate abroad...' into two short lines, one per route, and say in plain words what a Certificate of No Impediment proves.

Next to 'The celebration is where we come in', add one sentence on how the Wedded Advisor fits the celebration around the legal date (for Option A) or the local paperwork timeline (for Option B), so a parent knows the couple isn't juggling both alone.

checks.check: Every journey point, turn-off and CTA reaction has an exact quote from the draft
Stayed in character as Margaret (mother of the bride, paying about half, sent the link by her daughter, reads top to bottom on an iPad)
No invented brand facts; missing details listed as unanswered questions
HTML comments, image slots and VERIFY markers treated as invisible
Deferred business details (deposits, contracts, 2am contact) and transfers not raised as must-fix; absent prices, celebrant fees, translations and sourcing not raised as problems, per orchestrator
Journey types limited to the allowed enum; every turn-off has a why

open_questions.question: Main gaps for this persona: Option B is the densest section and the most decision-critical (readability turn-off); the destination takeaway bullet is overloaded; and a parent would like one line on how the Wedded Advisor coordinates the celebration with the legal timeline. Relevance is naturally moderate as this is a couple's paperwork topic. Call-first is a deferred business detail.

assumptions: Margaret's daughter is the bride and sent the link while deciding between marrying legally in Australia or abroad; Margaret reads the whole article on an iPad.
Prices, celebrant fees and translation details are deliberately absent and the brand does not discuss sourcing, so none were raised.
